steps.say: Cancer of the gallbladder grows where stones have irritated for years. Big stones, a chalky calcified wall and certain regions of the world carry far higher risk, with women affected most.
steps.tx: Gallstones over **3 cm** (three centimetres), **porcelain calcification** (chalky wall) and polyps over **10 mm** (ten millimetres) raise gallbladder cancer risk, endemic in North India with striking female predominance and late presentation at advanced stages with poor outlook unless caught early by chance.

vis.alt: Tumour at the gallbladder neck with stones, calcified wall and nearby draining glands.
vis.caption: Gallbladder cancer: tumour with gallstones, porcelain wall change and regional nodes. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A cancer found by accident after a routine removal behaves very differently by depth. Disease still in the lining needs nothing more, while muscle invasion demands a second, bigger operation.
steps.tx: Incidental **T1a** (mucosa-only) **incidental gallbladder cancer** (surprise early tumour) after simple cholecystectomy needs no further surgery with 5-year survival near **100 percent** (near total cure), while **T1b** (muscle invasion) needs extended resection with full nodal clearance for cure in fit surgical candidates.

steps.say: The second operation takes a rim of liver around the gallbladder bed plus all the nearby glands. A two-centimetre cuff of liver and a full packet of nodes turn an accident into a cure.
steps.tx: **Extended cholecystectomy** (liver-rim gallbladder removal) takes segments **IVb and V** (four B and five) with **2 cm** (two centimetre) margins plus **portal nodal clearance** (gland packet removal) of at least **6 nodes** (six glands) for T1b and T2 disease, converting surprise into cure.

steps.say: Tumours bursting through the wall but still removable go straight to extended resection, while cancers gripping big vessels start with drugs, not the knife. Only cancers that shrink and show no distant spread on repeat scans earn an operation.
steps.tx: Resectable **T3** (through-wall) disease breaching serosa goes straight to extended resection, while unresectable or borderline **T4** (vessel-gripping) disease with vascular invasion takes **neoadjuvant** (pre-surgery) gemcitabine-cisplatin first, with surgery only for responders without distant spread on careful restaging scans after chemotherapy courses finish fully.

steps.say: Yellow eyes at first visit usually mean the growth has reached the main pipes where no knife can follow. A metal tube placed through the blockage restores flow and buys months.
steps.tx: Jaundice at presentation usually marks unresectable hilar invasion, and palliation uses endoscopic **metal stenting** (spring tube drainage) with about 6 to **12 month** (often around **8 month**) patency plus pain and sepsis control by the palliative team throughout the remaining illness.

steps.say: Keyhole surgery for what looked like stones can scatter hidden cancer to the small cuts. Only a visibly involved scar is cut out together with the main specimen once pathology confirms the diagnosis.
steps.tx: **Port-site recurrence** (wound seeding after laparoscopy) for unsuspected cancer adds excision of visibly involved **port sites** (scar removal) only, since routine removal of all scars shows no survival benefit, together with the definitive resection specimen at radical reoperation without delay once the surprise diagnosis is fully confirmed by pathology review urgently.

steps.say: Even after a clean removal, tablets for half a year improve the odds. The BILCAP study supports this in per-protocol analysis, and close scanning catches the few recurrences early enough to act.
steps.tx: Adjuvant **capecitabine** (post-surgery tablets) for **6 months** (six months) after R0 resection improved survival in per-protocol analysis of **BILCAP** (adjuvant trial), with surveillance using **3-monthly** (quarterly) imaging in our protocol (NCCN suggests 6-monthly for 2 years) to catch the early recurrence peak when action still helps and cure remains possible after salvage.

steps.say: Not every thick-walled gallbladder is cancer. A fierce but benign inflammation swells the wall and sticks to everything nearby, so imaging clues plus a frozen sample during surgery tell the two apart.
steps.tx: **Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis** (granuloma wall disease) mimics cancer with wall thickening and infiltration, distinguished by intact mucosa on imaging and **frozen section** (instant microscopy) at surgery before any radical steps are taken, since mimics such as porcelain gallbladder also thicken the wall.

vis.caption: Porcelain gallbladder with mural calcium, a benign cancer mimic set beside XGC on imaging. Credit: StewardMD.
